title: Zelenskyy Says Russia Struck Energy Sites Hours After Trump Announced Ceasefire
excerpt: Ukraine held its fire overnight, Zelenskyy told Fox News, while a strike on a Kharkiv power plant killed three. Moscow has not confirmed it accepted any energy ceasefire.
body:
• President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Russia attacked Ukraine's gas and energy infrastructure hours after President Donald Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between the two countries.
  • Ukraine held its fire on Russian energy targets overnight, Zelenskyy told Fox News, while a strike on a Kharkiv power plant killed three people and wounded nine, including children.
  • Moscow has not confirmed accepting any energy ceasefire, and Russian officials communicated that they knew nothing about one, Zelenskyy said.
  • Kyiv is asking Washington for greater pressure on Moscow as winter approaches and Ukraine's power grid faces a renewed strike campaign.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Vladimir Putin on Monday of defying President Donald Trump's ceasefire push, saying Russian forces struck Ukraine's energy infrastructure within hours of Trump's announcement that both sides had agreed to stop attacking energy facilities.

"We are ready today for energy ceasefire, as President Trump said. But I'm not sure that Putin is ready because even after yesterday's messages from the president about energy cease fire, Putin attacked our gas infrastructure," Zelenskyy told Fox News in a live interview on "America's Newsroom." Asked whether Ukraine would honour the truce, he said Kyiv already had: Ukraine refrained from striking Russian energy facilities overnight.

The Kharkiv strike

Speaking earlier at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, Zelenskyy said a Kharkiv power plant was hit on Sunday night in a large-scale attack on the region that killed three people and wounded nine others, including children. Photographs from Kharkiv on Monday showed a residential building burning after a Russian air attack. Zelenskyy described the strikes as Putin's direct answer to Trump's initiative: "It was his answer to President Trump. He attacked our energy infrastructure."

"The communication from Russia was very clear that they don't know anything about energy ceasefire."

— Volodymyr Zelenskyy, President of Ukraine

A ceasefire only one side announced

Trump announced the energy ceasefire on Sunday in a post on Truth Social, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate halt to attacks on energy facilities. Moscow has not confirmed accepting such an agreement, and the precise scope of the proposal remains disputed. The announcement landed alongside Trump's push for a deal under which the United States would buy large amounts of Russian diesel to combat surging fuel costs — a plan Zelenskyy has criticised as a gift to Putin. Russia has not publicly responded to Zelenskyy's specific charge that it violated the truce overnight.

Why energy is the battleground

Energy infrastructure has been a central target throughout the war. Strikes on power plants, substations and gas facilities in the run-up to winter threaten heating and electricity for millions of Ukrainians, while Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and depots have squeezed Moscow's fuel supply. An energy-only truce would be narrower than a full ceasefire, but it is the one measure both sides have previously observed for limited periods — and the one Kyiv says Moscow has now broken before it began.

What comes next

Zelenskyy's message was aimed at the White House as much as at Moscow: he urged the United States to increase pressure on Russia, arguing that only American leverage will move Putin. Whether Washington treats the Kharkiv strike as a violation — and what consequences, if any, follow — is the test of the arrangement Trump announced. For now, the ceasefire exists as an American announcement, a Ukrainian commitment and a Russian silence punctuated by missiles.
